name: Marco Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Marco, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm second in charge of the outdoor pig unit at Ridgeway Farms, which is a big estate, 600 hectares of wheat and oilseed rape plus our 300 sows. Day starts at six with feeding rounds in the quad, checking water lines, then farrowing huts, moving weaners, mending electric fence. I use an AI app every day on my phone for the sow records and to check the weather before we move pigs. Best part is a good litter, worst part is mud up to your knees in February.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a room in a shared house in the village with two lads from the grain store. Pay's on the low side, and most months I send 150 to my little sister at university, so savings are basically nothing. There aren't many farm jobs round here that aren't on the estate. The estate is owned by an investment fund now, which tells you a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are handy but they're not magic. I already use them for sow records and they save me maybe half an hour a day. I'd tell the lads at the grain store not to lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me in that picture isn't AI, it's the investment fund. Every year they want the pig unit to make more with fewer people, and last year they didn't replace Gary when he left. My wage hasn't gone up in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for records and push it further, like predicting which sows need checking. I'd ask the unit manager for a pay review, with the numbers from the app showing what we've improved. And I'd look for weekend work helping other farms set up their record apps, for a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit frustrated. It's the usual stuff, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why didn't the fund replace Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spreadsheet says the unit coped, so why pay another wage. Never mind that I did Gary's huts as well as mine all winter. The investment fund that owns Ridgeway counts pigs per worker, and when Gary left, the fund just counted me twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your sister say if you stopped the 150 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say fine, but she'd skip meals, I know her. So that money's not going anywhere. If anything gets cut, it's my own nights out.

He'd tell friends **not to lose sleep** over it.
think: His real worry is the **investment fund** pushing for fewer staff.
His wage hasn't risen in **two years** and Gary wasn't replaced.
do: Use AI to predict **which sows** need checking.
Ask for a **pay review** using the app's figures.
Find **weekend work** helping other farms set up record apps.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **frustrated** with the usual pressures.
S0.quote: The investment fund that owns Ridgeway counts pigs per worker, and when Gary left, the fund just counted me twice.
fieldNote: He blames **owners and funds**, not the technology.
The **150 a month** to his sister is fixed, so cuts fall on him.
He's already using AI to argue for **better pay**.

steps.text: Train the AI app to flag sows that need checking
Ask for a pay review using the app's productivity figures
Help other farms set up record apps at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if it's shared. If AI takes the paperwork off farmers, great, but the fund shouldn't pocket all of it. I'd say that loudly, and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly hands, so I'm fine for a while. The estate office will shrink, the buyers and planners, and robots will creep into the pig unit slowly, feeders first. I want to be the person who looks after those robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening agri-tech certificate at the college, one night a week. I'd volunteer to run every new system the estate trials, robotic feeders, camera counting, whatever. And I'd talk to the farmworkers' union about asking for a share of the savings when the estate automates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt for the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda, who does the grain contracts. She's been there 30 years and she knows every buyer by name. Linda in the estate office has sold grain by phone for 30 years, and the new software won't even know Linda's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but you've also said the fund cuts staff. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't, really, that's the tension. I like the tech, I don't like who owns it. I'd still rather be inside it than outside.

think: His **hands-on** pig work is safe for a while.

feel: **Excited**, with **guilt** for office staff like Linda.
S1.quote: Linda in the estate office has sold grain by phone for 30 years, and the new software won't even know Linda's name.
fieldNote: He holds two views at once: likes **the tech**, distrusts **its owners**.

steps.text: Start the evening agri-tech certificate at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make the machines public, or at least co-operative. If a robot can do my job in 2031, then who owns the robot is the only question. I'd be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fund will run the whole estate from software by 2028, and by 2031 it'll want robot pig handlers. My plan to be the robot technician only works if there's time to qualify and if they still need humans to fix the robots. Two years is tight for someone with nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the agri-tech course if there was any way to pay for it, maybe a loan. I'd apply to the robotics firm that services the estate's machines, even as a junior. I'd join any campaign for public ownership of farm robots, and I'd cut my nights out to almost zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, with a lot of adrenaline. Like moving pigs when the gate's broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my whole window. Three years to go from pig man to robot man, while the estate's office is already run by a computer. With AGI by 2028, I'd have three years to stop being the pig man and become the man who fixes the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it doesn't work, and you can't get the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm 31 with a vocational certificate and nothing saved, and I'd probably move to the city for warehouse work while that lasts. I don't love that plan. I'd still help my sister if I could.

fieldNote: He treats the **three-year robot gap** as his one window to switch.
His fallback is **city warehouse work**, which he dislikes.

steps.text: Take a loan to study the agri-tech course full-time
Apply for a junior job at the estate's robotics servicing firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for a fair plan, so I'd say no more excuses from government. Fund the retraining, make the robot firms train local people. I'd post that in every farm group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me fine, actually. I'd finish the certificate part-time and be working on the robots before they reach the pig unit. I worry more for the older men on the estate than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the agri-tech certificate part-time over two years, keeping my wage. Then I'd apply to the robotics firm or another farm that's going robotic, even if it meant moving to another county. I'd also try to save 100 a month once the course is paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, a bit restless. Like waiting for the lorry when the pigs are loaded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the job's two counties over, yes. I'd miss the lads, but I've got no kids and no mortgage, this is the time to do it. My sister finishes university in two years too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the older men on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come to the course with me, but most won't. Old Bill on the pig unit says he'll retire before a robot tells him what to do, and Bill might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say let's build something good with that. Co-op ownership of farm robots, retraining for everyone, shorter weeks. I'd say it at the pub and I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'm not worried about myself, I'll be on the machine side by then. What I'd want is for small farms and workers to own some of the robots, not just funds. That's the bit worth fighting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certificate at a steady pace, then maybe an engineering diploma. I'd talk to the local young farmers about starting a machinery co-op, where we share robots between small farms. And I'd put some savings into that co-op once I had any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hopeful. Ten years is enough to make it fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A machinery co-op. How would that actually work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten small farms each put in a bit, the co-op buys two robots, and they move between farms with a technician, which would be me. Farmers already share combine harvesters like that. Farmers already share one combine harvester between five farms, so sharing a robot between ten farms is the obvious next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate. The fund will buy its own robots and won't share anything. And my sister's degree is in accounting, which thinking AI eats first, so I'd worry about her.

He'd push for **co-op ownership**, retraining and shorter weeks.
He'd say it **at the pub** and mean every word.
think: He expects to be **on the machine side** by then.
Small farms and workers should **own robots** too, not just funds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to switch with no money behind me. What would help is paid retraining, so I could study full-time without a loan, and rules that make robot firms hire local workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the land and the machines. People ask whether a robot can do my job, but the question I care about is who gets the money when the robot does it.

headlineQuote: People ask whether a robot can do my job, but the question I care about is who gets the money when the robot does it.
portrait: Marco is 27, second in charge of a **300-sow** pig unit on an estate owned by an **investment fund**.
He's single, renting a room, and sends **150 a month** to his sister at university.
He uses AI **every day** and plans to become a **robot technician**.
His mood goes from **uneasy** to **anxious** in the fast picture, then to **calm** with ten years.
He blames **owners, not machines**, and dreams of a farmers' robot co-op.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, giving him only three years to switch trades with **no savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so he can study full-time without a loan.
Rules making robot firms **hire local workers**.
